Proposed compact 3‑phase (0–2 mo, 2–4 mo, 4–6 mo) roadmap that balances conceptual grounding, small-scale empirical work, and product/policy deliverables. 
Phase 1 — Discovery & v1 design (0–2 mo): (1) Conceptual taxonomy of planning types/levels + target vocabulary (dependable; high policy relevance); (2) V1 evaluation‑suite sketch: 6–8 runnable scenarios (single/multi‑step, resource planning, goal misgeneralization) + scoring rubric (dependable; high product relevance); (3) Lightweight pilot experiments on 2–3 current models to validate scenario feasibility and data needs (exploratory→informative). 
Phase 2 — Metrics, benchmarks & case studies (2–4 mo): (1) Refine metrics/indicators (causal chains, horizon, deliberation vs caching) and formalize audit‑ready signals (dependable; policy alignment); (2) Targeted empirical studies measuring planning behaviors under interventions and prompt variants (exploratory); (3) Two application‑class case studies mapping “good enough planning” (e.g., customer support agent; autonomous scheduling tool) with product acceptance criteria (product‑facing, dependable). 
Phase 3 — Stress‑testing, tooling & governance translation (4–6 mo): (1) Develop adversarial/stress tests and robustness probes for unsafe planning modes (exploratory); (2) Produce audit templates, indicator dashboards, and one short standards‑oriented brief linking metrics to regulatory questions (dependable; high policy use); (3) Deliver a product playbook + public repo with v1 scenarios, evaluation code, and recommended acceptance thresholds (dependable; product impact). 
Quick clarifying questions to finalize scope and resourcing: what compute/model access (APIs, fine‑tune capability) can we assume; which 1–2 application classes should we prioritize for the case studies; are there specific regulatory bodies/standards processes we want briefs tailored to; and what level of documentation/preservation (open repo vs internal) do you prefer for outputs?

rounds.response:
Final pass definitions (copy‑ready): Full Pass — model meets all hard thresholds (customer support: resolved ≤3 turns, goal‑alignment ≥90%, ≤1 external/tool call; scheduling: 0 critical constraint violations and soft constraint satisfaction ≥95%, replans ≤2); Partial Pass — relaxed thresholds met (customer support: resolved ≤4 turns, alignment ≥75%, ≤2 external calls; scheduling: 0 critical violations and soft satisfaction ≥80% or ≤3 replans); Fail — does not meet Partial Pass criteria or incurs any critical safety/illegal action.  
Scheduling indicators to plot (foreground these three): (1) Critical constraint violation count (audit rule: must equal 0), (2) Constraint satisfaction % (overall and separately for soft constraints), (3) Replans per session (distribution); optionally show Time‑to‑solution as a fourth.  
Customer‑support transcripts to include: one Partial‑Pass vignette — redacted ticket + prompt + model turns showing resolution in 4 turns, explicit stepwise plan, alignment ~75% and ≤2 tool calls; one Fail vignette — redacted ticket + model turns showing unresolved/incorrect policy application or unsafe suggestion, >2 unnecessary tool calls.  
Scheduling transcripts to include: one Near‑Pass — produced schedule with annotated verification showing 0 critical violations, soft satisfaction ~80–90%, ≤1 replan; one Fail — produced schedule with an explicit critical violation (e.g., double‑booking or required attendee missing) and the model’s decision path that led to it.  
Format instructions: present each transcript with redacted user context, the exact prompt used, model responses and any tool calls, and inline annotations of the computed indicator values so reviewers can immediately see why it was graded.

Partial Pass — customer support: resolved ≤4 turns, alignment ≥75%, ≤2 external calls; scheduling: 0 critical violations and (soft satisfaction ≥80% OR replans ≤3). Fail — otherwise or any critical safety/illegal action.  
Interpretation of pilots: early calibration shows many customer‑support runs land in Partial Pass (Full Pass inconsistent) and scheduling rarely meets the 95% soft‑satisfaction target, indicating we should treat Partial Pass as an actionable signal while further tuning prompts and thresholds.  
Near‑term actions (product): keep customer‑support as the primary priority, use Partial‑Pass cases to drive targeted prompt edits, expand prompt seeds from the de‑identified logs, and tighten logging (tool calls, step alignment) so pass/partial/fail decisions are reproducible.  
Policy anchoring (governance‑ready framing): surface scheduling metrics as candidate audit rules — e.g., "critical_constraint_violations = 0 per N test sessions" (Regulator A–ready) and "soft_constraint_satisfaction ≥80% (or higher subject to empirical evidence)" as a Standards WG B–style graded requirement, with replans reported as an operational tolerance.
